newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch hail Australian mercy death, mull own law.
newsitem.headline: Dutch hail Australian mercy death, mull own law.

text.p: Dutch right-to-die campaigners on Thursday hailed the legally assisted suicide of a terminally ill Australian cancer patient as a victory for personal freedom.
"We think it is fantastic that doctors were able to legally honour the patient's last request," said Jonne Boesjes of the influential Dutch Voluntary Euthanasia Society.

Bob Dent, a prostate cancer patient in his mid-60s, became the world's first legally-assisted suicide when he was given a lethal injection under controversial mercy killing legislation introduced in July in Australia's Northern Territory.

The Dutch Justice Ministry said the landmark death was unlikely to speed up government deliberations over whether to legalise euthanasia in the Netherlands, where some 1,500 cases of mercy killing are reported annually.
"We have our own legal proceedings and what happens abroad will not affect the decision-making here," a Justice Ministry spokesman said.
Although technically illegal, euthanasia is tolerated under Dutch law if certain guidelines are followed.
Doctors are virtually assured of freedom from prosecution if the patient was of sound mind, in unbearable physical or mental pain and had repeatedly asked for death.
Before ending a patient's life, a doctor has to consult a second, independent physician. The whole process must be documented and reported under special disclosure procedures introduced in 1993.
Public acceptance of euthanasia is widespread, with a poll earlier this year showing that 84 percent of Dutch people supported the practice to relieve unbearable and irremediable suffering.
However death-on-demand campaigners say existing procedures do not give doctors sufficient legal protection, arguing successive administrations have interpreted the guidelines differently.
As a result, they argue, patients in need are being refused the right to die by doctors fearful of prosecution.
The current three-party coalition will review the need for new euthanasia legislation based on the outcome of an inquiry into existing reporting procedures.

The report of the inquiry, due to have been presented in October, has been delayed until November, virtually ruling out the prospect of new legislation during the current cabinet term, the Justice Ministry spokesman said.
"The current administration has one and a half years to run, I think one can assume that there will be no new euthanasia law within that time," he said.
If current euthanasia practice is legalised in the Netherlands, Dutch legislation will reach far beyond Australia's, where right-to-die laws extend only to the terminally ill.
Dutch jurisprudence on the issue so far indicates doctors will legitimately be able to end the life of people who are not terminally ill or even physically infirm.

In 1994 the Dutch Supreme Court upheld the right of a psychiatrist to end the life of a physically healthy woman who lost the will to live after she divorced and her sons died, ruling that unbearable mental suffering also constituted sufficient grounds for euthanasia.

The scope of Dutch mercy-killing laws were further widened last year, after a doctor was held to have acted justifiably in ending the life of a severely handicapped baby girl in consulation with her parents.
